relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

relation_context.previous_passage_tail:
eplied Utterson. “I have a document here in his handwriting; it is between ourselves, for I scarce know what to do about it; it is an ugly business at the best. But there it is; quite in your way: a murderer’s autograph.”
[P27] Guest’s eyes brightened, and he sat down at once and studied it with passion. “No sir,” he said: “not mad; but it is an odd hand.”
[P28] “And by all accounts a very odd writer,” added the lawyer.
[P29] Just then the servant entered with a note.
[P30] “Is that from Dr. Jekyll, sir?” inquired the clerk. “I thought I knew the writing. Anything private, Mr. Utterson?”
[P31] “Only an invitation to dinner. Why? Do you want to see it?”
[P32] “One moment. I thank you, sir;” and the clerk laid the two sheets of paper alongside and sedulously compared their contents. “Thank you, sir,” he said at last, returning both; “it’s a very interesting autograph.”
[P33] There was a pause, during which Mr. Utterson struggled with himself. “Why did you compare them, Guest?” he inquired suddenly.
[P34] “Well, sir,” returned the clerk, “there’s a rather singular resemblance; the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped.”
[P35] “Rather quaint,” said Utterson.
[P36] “It is, as you say, rather quaint,” returned Guest.
[P37] “I wouldn’t speak of this note, you know,” said the master.
[P38] “No, sir,” said the clerk. “I understand.”
[P39] But no sooner was Mr. Utterson alone that night, than he locked the note into his safe, where it reposed from that time forward. “What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold in his veins.

known_before.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, living in Soho and served by Poole and an old woman landlady. He is merciless and inspires enduring hatred, impressing beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled a girl and paid a hundred pounds with a cheque. Utterson later accosted him at the by-street door, and Hyde gave his Soho address before disappearing inside. Jekyll called him poor Hyde and asked Utterson to help him. The maid then saw Hyde beat Sir Danvers Carew to death

known_before.name: Dr. Lanyon
known_before.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor
known_before.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old school and college friend of Mr. Utterson and a friend of Dr. Jekyll. He is hearty, red-faced, prematurely white-haired, boisterous, decided, theatrical but genuine. Utterson came to consult him about Jekyll's will and Hyde. Lanyon welcomed him warmly, said Jekyll had become too fanciful and wrong in mind over ten years ago, and had never heard of Hyde. He now remains Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor, unaware of Hyde's identity.

known_before.bio: Poole is the elderly servant and butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, serving his master Dr. Jekyll and obeying the man in the middle as an obeyed superior. He admitted Utterson to Jekyll's house and told him Jekyll had gone out. He confirmed that Hyde has a key and comes by the dissecting room door, that all servants have orders to obey Hyde, and that Hyde never dines there and mostly uses the laboratory. He now continues in his post, bound by orders to obey Hyde.
